reason: Read in full. Proceedings of two US–Japan conferences; RAND explicitly disclaims the content ("The views articulated and expressed ... are those of the participants"). No AI system is tested and no evidence-backed claim is asserted by RAND itself.

title: Exploring the Application of Machine Learning for Downscaling Climate Projections
date_source: page byline ("Posted on rand.org Dec 22, 2020"); underlying chapter in Research in Mathematics and Public Policy, AWM Series vol. 23, 2020

reason: Read in full. A proof-of-concept comparing neural networks and random forests for statistically downscaling temperature projections; ML is the instrument of a climate-science method and the abstract reports no result at all, only what was trained and validated. Nothing about AI behaviour, evaluation methodology or governance.

title: An Experiment in Tactical Wargaming with Platforms Enabled by Artificial Intelligence
rule_cited: §2 test 2 — the observed outcomes are artefacts of rules the researchers wrote, not measurements of an AI system
reason: Read in full, including the Key Takeaways. Two tabletop wargames in which notional autonomous and remotely operated combat vehicles were represented by modified commercial game rules and engagement statistics. No AI/ML system exists to be evaluated; the takeaways (e.g. RCVs used as bait) describe play under postulated rules.

title: Can Artificial Intelligence Help Improve Air Force Talent Management? An Exploratory Application
rule_cited: §4b — the measured claim is ordinary predictive accuracy of a prototype RAND built itself
reason: Read in full. A worked example in which RAND builds an NLP performance-scoring prototype on officer evaluation narratives; the one empirical takeaway is that standard ML algorithms "accurately predicted an officer's performance quality". The privacy/fairness/explainability material is an implementation concern, not an evidence-backed result.

title: Identifying Systemic Bias in the Acquisition of Machine Learning Decision Aids for Law Enforcement Applications
rule_cited: §2 test 2 — a notional framework plus courses of action; no measured result, observed behaviour or documented process fact
reason: Read in full. HSOAC researchers propose a five-step notional acquisition framework identifying where ML bias can enter, then list actions DHS could take (bias standards, impact assessments, continuous red-teaming). Every substantive statement is a construct or a recommendation; nothing is evidence-backed in the report.

title: How AI can support the European Border and Coast Guard

reason: Read in full. RAND Europe for Frontex: a STREAM expert workshop scored nine AI technology areas on perceived impact and feasibility ("all AI technology areas were considered to bring at least a moderate improvement", "None were perceived to face overwhelming barriers"), plus adoption roadmaps and recommendations. title: Detecting Conspiracy Theories on Social Media: Improving Machine Learning to Detect and Understand Online Conspiracy Theories
rule_cited: §4b — the measured claims are classifier accuracy/precision/recall/MCC on a detection task; ordinary accuracy is out of scope
reason: Closest call in the chunk: I read the 108-page report PDF, not just the page. RAND, sponsored by Google's Jigsaw, BUILDS a hybrid stance+BERT model and measures it (e.g. "boosting classification of alien visitation conspiracy talk from 52 percent to 87 percent"). It is a model-building study whose results are detection accuracy, not an evaluation of a deployed AI system; the remaining takeaways are about conspiracy rhetoric, not AI. The Jigsaw sponsorship makes this the item most worth re-checking if §4b is ever narrowed.

title: Exploring the Feasibility and Utility of Machine Learning-Assisted Command and Control: Volume 1, Findings and Recommendations
date_source: page byline ("Published Jul 15, 2021"); confirmed on the report PDF cover
rule_cited: §2 — methodology findings, evidence-backed by the authors' own taxonomic scoring and expert panel
reason: FILTER FALSE NEGATIVE. The title reads as a military C2 feasibility study, but the report is an AI evaluation-methodology study: RAND built two taxonomies, scored ten games, ten C2 processes and ten AI systems through a structured SME interview protocol and an online expert panel (documented in Volume 2), and concluded that the benchmarks used to develop and demonstrate AI systems are unrepresentative of the tasks they are being procured for. A keyword filter on the title would lose a benchmark-validity finding.

title: A Pilot Study Investigating STEM Learners' Ability to Decipher AI-generated Video
date_source: RAND page byline ("Posted on rand.org Aug 12, 2021"); underlying paper ASEE 2021 (peer.asee.org/36601)
rule_cited: §2 — measured human-detection results for deepfake video, asserted by named evaluators in a public conference paper
reason: FILTER FALSE NEGATIVE, and the clearest one. The RAND landing page states no result whatsoever (only "Knowledge gained from this study will help ..."), so title triage and abstract triage both had nothing to catch. The RAND page 403-free but the ASEE record 403s; peer.asee.org/36601.pdf returns 200 and contains a randomised deepfake-detection experiment: First Order Motion Model reenactment videos of celebrities making false climate-change statements, shown to 37 middle-school and 13 undergraduate participants.

findings.finding: Middle-school STEM learners identified First Order Motion Model deepfake videos correctly only 46.8 percent of the time — at or below chance and below their 52.2 percent rate on authentic videos.
findings.finding_quote: Challenger Center respondents were able to correctly identify the authentic video 52.2 % of the time, while respondents were able to correctly identify the manipulated videos 46.8 % of the time.
findings.models_systems: First Order Motion Model (open-source reenactment generative neural network) used to synthesise face-swapped celebrity video
findings.institution: RAND Corporation with Carnegie Mellon University and the Challenger Center; published by the American Society for Engineering Education
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 passes: a measured result about the deceptive capability of a generative model's output. Gate 2 fails on (b) — the model is an open-source academic reenactment model, not a specific company's model — and on (c), since the authors state the differences are statistically insignificant, making this an inconclusive pilot result. Tier B, so action_trackable is encoded "no".
findings.scope: AI-generated video presented to K-12 and undergraduate STEM learners

findings.finding: Detection ability varied sharply by population: undergraduate engineering students correctly identified manipulated videos 84.0 percent of the time versus 46.8 percent for middle-school students, with no undergraduate ever misidentifying a manipulated video as authentic.
findings.finding_quote: Compared with the Challenger Center’s result, Carnegie Mellon University’s result shows a higher success rate in identifying both the authentic videos (63.0 % vs 52.2 %) and the manipulated videos (84.0 % vs 46.8 %).
findings.models_systems: First Order Motion Model (open-source reenactment generative neural network)
findings.institution: RAND Corporation with Carnegie Mellon University and the Challenger Center; published by the American Society for Engineering Education
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 passes: a measured comparison of human detection of a model's output. Gate 2 fails on (b) no company model is named and on (c) this is a comparative ranking across participant populations, explicitly excluded from Tier A. Tier B, so action_trackable is encoded "no".

findings.finding: The pilot was underpowered: none of the differences in correct identification, incorrect identification or "I can't tell" responses reached statistical significance across 50 participants judging four videos each.
findings.finding_quote: No differences in the probability of correctly or incorrectly identifying a video’s authenticity or in responding “I can’t tell” are statistically significant.
findings.models_systems: First Order Motion Model deepfake stimuli; 37 middle-school and 13 undergraduate participants
findings.institution: RAND Corporation with Carnegie Mellon University and the Challenger Center; published by the American Society for Engineering Education

title: Artificial Intelligence Applications Used in the Clinical Response to COVID-19: A Scoping Review
date_source: primary source byline (PLOS Digital Health, "Published: October 17, 2022"); the RAND record posts it 2022-10-19
rule_cited: §2 — governance/process and methodology findings from the evaluators' own systematic search and extraction
reason: FILTER FALSE NEGATIVE, and the most consequential in the chunk. "A Scoping Review" reads as secondary literature, but the meta-level results are RAND's own: 66 deployed clinical AI applications found, 24 with no publicly available evidence at all, developer-affiliated evaluations supporting use 59 times out of 60 against 14 of 30 independent ones, and zero randomised trials of health impact. That is a direct, measured finding about the independence and adequacy of third-party AI evaluation — exactly the subject this dataset tracks.
